Scope

This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge regarding adsorbents for gas drying, a process of considerable industrial importance in which water vapour is removed from a gas stream by means of a solid adsorbent that captures the water and is subsequently regenerated so that it can be used again. The review draws on 87 papers published over the course of the last 9 years. The adsorbents falling within the scope of the review are silica gel, activated alumina, and molecular sieves, which together represent the principal families in routine drying service. The gases considered include natural gas, air, hydrogen, and light hydrocarbon streams, in all of which water is removed for a variety of reasons, including the protection of equipment, compliance with product specifications, and the prevention of hydrate formation and corrosion in cold equipment. Studies concerned with liquid-phase drying, membrane separation, and absorption into liquid solvents are excluded from consideration. The evidence base comprises three main types of study: isotherm measurements of water uptake, breakthrough tests conducted on packed beds, and cyclic tests in which uptake is tracked across regeneration steps. It is important to emphasise that a paper is treated as evidence for a performance claim only where the gas, the temperature range, and the regeneration conditions are clearly stated, since drying performance is fundamentally a property of the adsorbent operating within its duty, rather than of the adsorbent in isolation. The review is structured around what the literature collectively establishes, where it disagrees, and what it leaves unmeasured.

Established results

It is widely recognised that water uptake at low partial pressure is the characteristic that most clearly separates the families. Molecular sieves exhibit a strong uptake of water at low partial pressure, a behaviour that can be attributed to their pore openings, which admit water while excluding much of what travels with it, and to their extensive internal surface, which retains water even against a dry stream. Silica gel and activated alumina, by contrast, take up considerably less under the same dry conditions, although their uptake increases substantially as the gas approaches saturation, at which point condensation within the wider pores begins to supplement adsorption on the surface. Across the range covered by the literature, this ordering is not reversed: where the driest outlets are required, molecular sieves retain a clear advantage, although that advantage progressively narrows as the outlet requirement is relaxed. Outlet dryness is consequently a matter of selecting between families before it becomes a question of bed sizing, and beds of gel or alumina are typically sized larger for the same dry duty rather than being expected to match the performance of a sieve at low partial pressure.

Regeneration can be accomplished by heating, by pressure release, or by means of a dry purge gas, and every family is regenerated by at least one of these routes in commercial practice. Heating a saturated bed drives off the accumulated water and restores the greater part of its uptake capacity. The extent of restoration depends both on the temperature achieved and on the completeness with which the bed is cooled before being returned to service. A bed that is returned to service while still warm will take up less water during the subsequent cycle, and a number of papers attribute early breakthrough to incomplete cooling rather than to any genuine deterioration of the adsorbent, underscoring the point that cooling should properly be regarded as an integral part of the regeneration step rather than as an idle interval, and that cycle designs which shorten the cooling step effectively trade capacity for cycle time.

Breakthrough behaviour, meanwhile, follows a broadly consistent pattern across all three families. A mass-transfer zone is established at the inlet of the bed and migrates through it, and the outlet remains dry until such time as the zone reaches the bed outlet. The length of this zone increases with gas velocity and particle size, and decreases as the affinity for water becomes stronger. Because adsorption releases heat, the bed warms as the zone passes through it, and this warming reduces the local uptake, with the result that a rapidly loaded bed will break through earlier than a prediction based on the cold isotherm would suggest. Studies that record bed temperature alongside outlet moisture show the two quantities moving in tandem, highlighting the risk that designs which neglect the temperature rise will systematically overstate the useful cycle time.

Binders, furthermore, act to dilute capacity. Molecular sieve crystals are formed into beads and pellets with the assistance of a binder, and since the binder itself adsorbs very little water, a formed adsorbent inevitably exhibits a lower uptake per unit mass than the crystal from which it is manufactured. Where papers report crystal and formed material side by side, the formed material is consistently found to be lower in uptake and slower in its approach to equilibrium. Mechanical degradation occurs through attrition in cycled beds and through dusting during handling, and the resulting dust increases the pressure drop across the bed while also posing a fouling risk to downstream equipment. The slower degradation mechanism is hydrothermal in nature: repeated regeneration in the presence of water vapour progressively reduces the uptake of alumina and silica gel, with the loss proceeding more rapidly at higher regeneration temperatures. Heavy hydrocarbons present in the feed introduce an additional fouling pathway, since they adsorb strongly, are only incompletely removed at regeneration temperatures selected for water, and can obstruct pores against water in subsequent cycles.

Disagreements

The literature is notably divided on the equilibrium water uptake of molecular sieves at low partial pressure. Although the quantity is nominally the same in each case, namely the uptake per unit mass at a stated low partial pressure and temperature, the values reported for comparable materials diverge by margins that are too substantial to be dismissed as experimental scatter. On closer inspection, the conflict appears to track the measurement route adopted. Gravimetric measurements, in which a sample is exposed to a stream of controlled humidity until its mass stabilises, tend to yield the higher values. Values derived from breakthrough curves, on the other hand, tend to emerge lower, and the derivation itself depends on the assumed shape of the mass-transfer zone, meaning that a portion of the discrepancy is embedded in the calculation rather than measured directly. Equilibration time constitutes a second source of disagreement. At low partial pressure the uptake process is slow, and a measurement terminated at a predetermined time may capture a point on the trajectory towards equilibrium rather than equilibrium itself. Papers differ considerably in whether a steady reading was awaited, and the shorter tests systematically report lower uptakes. Pretreatment represents a third source: a sample that has been regenerated more aggressively prior to testing begins from a drier state and consequently adsorbs more, so the reported uptake partly reflects the regeneration the sample happened to receive. Formed and crystal samples are also intermingled in the comparisons, and the binder fraction alone is sufficient to shift the reported values. The disagreement is therefore best understood as a disagreement about method before it is a disagreement about materials, and it cannot be resolved on the basis of the published values alone, since the papers do not report their conditions on a common basis, and no two of the conflicting reports simultaneously share the same route, equilibration criterion, and pretreatment.

Gaps

Perhaps the most striking omission in the literature is that the measurement nobody reports is the retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling: that is, the water uptake of a formed adsorbent measured once more after the material has been regenerated many times under the conditions of its own intended duty. The literature reports fresh uptake in abundance, and ageing studies report uptake following steaming, storage, or exposure to a contaminant, but the cycled measurement, performed on the material that would actually be purchased, under the regeneration regime that the unit would actually apply, is conspicuously absent. This gap is of practical significance, because the selection between families ultimately turns on service life just as much as on fresh capacity. A family exhibiting the higher fresh uptake but the faster cyclic loss may well prove more expensive over the lifetime of a charge than a family that starts lower and retains its uptake, and at present that comparison simply cannot be performed on the basis of measurements, leaving purchasers to price the associated risk from warranty terms instead. A second gap follows naturally from the first: no paper reports uptake and mechanical condition together following cycling, and so the balance between capacity loss and attrition loss within one and the same charge remains unquantified, meaning that a bed may be retired on account of dust while its uptake is still sound, or alternatively retained in service on account of its uptake while its dust burdens the downstream equipment. Until the cycled measurement becomes available on a common basis, comparisons between the families will continue to rest on fresh material, and every judgement regarding selection in this review must be read subject to that limitation.

Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying: the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by a solid that takes up the water and is regenerated for reuse. The review covers 87 papers from the last 9 years. The adsorbents in scope are silica gel, activated alumina, and molecular sieves, the families in routine drying service. The gases in scope are natural gas, air, hydrogen, and light hydrocarbon streams, where water is removed to protect equipment, to meet a product specification, or to prevent hydrate formation and corrosion in cold equipment. Papers on liquid-phase drying, on membranes, and on absorption into a liquid solvent fall outside the scope. The evidence admitted is of three kinds: isotherm measurements of water uptake, breakthrough tests on packed beds, and cyclic tests in which uptake is followed across regeneration. A paper counts as evidence for a performance claim only where its gas, its temperature range, and its regeneration conditions are stated, because drying performance is a property of the adsorbent and its duty together, never of the adsorbent alone. The review is organised by what the papers establish jointly, where they conflict, and what they leave unmeasured.

Established results

Water uptake at low partial pressure separates the families. Molecular sieves take up water strongly at low partial pressure, because their pore openings admit water and exclude much of what travels with it, and their internal surface holds water against a dry stream. Silica gel and activated alumina take up less under the same dry conditions and take up more as the gas approaches saturation, where condensation inside the wider pores adds to uptake on the surface. The ordering reverses nowhere in the range the papers cover: for the driest outlets the molecular sieves hold the advantage, and the advantage narrows as the outlet requirement relaxes. Outlet dryness is therefore a selection between families before it is a question of bed size, and beds of gel or alumina are sized larger for the same dry duty rather than expected to match the sieve at low partial pressure.

Regeneration is by heat, by pressure release, or by a dry purge, and every family is regenerated by at least one of the three in commercial units. Heating a saturated bed drives the water off and restores most of the uptake. The restored amount depends on the temperature the bed reaches and on how completely the bed is cooled before it returns to service. A bed returned warm takes up less water in the next cycle, and several papers trace early breakthrough to incomplete cooling rather than to any loss of adsorbent capacity. Cooling is thus part of the regeneration step, not a pause after it, and cycle designs that shorten cooling buy cycle time with capacity.

Breakthrough behaviour follows one pattern across the families. A mass-transfer zone forms at the bed inlet and travels through the bed, and the outlet stays dry until the zone reaches it. The zone lengthens with gas velocity and with particle size, and shortens as the affinity for water strengthens. Uptake releases heat, and the bed warms as the zone passes; the warming lowers the local uptake, so a fast-loaded bed breaks through earlier than its cold isotherm promises. Papers that measure bed temperature alongside outlet moisture report the two moving together, and designs that ignore the temperature rise overstate the useful cycle time.

Binders dilute capacity. Molecular sieve crystals are formed into beads and pellets with a binder, and the binder takes up little water, so a formed adsorbent takes up less per unit mass than the crystal it is made from. Papers that report crystal and formed material side by side put the formed material lower on uptake and slower on the approach to equilibrium. Mechanical degradation is by attrition in cycled beds and by dusting in handling; the dust raises the pressure drop across the bed and can foul the equipment downstream. The slow loss is hydrothermal: repeated regeneration in the presence of water vapour reduces the uptake of alumina and of silica gel over time, and the loss runs faster at higher regeneration temperatures. Heavy hydrocarbons in the feed add a second fouling route, because they adsorb strongly, are driven off incompletely at regeneration temperatures set for water, and block pores against water in later cycles.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake of molecular sieves at low partial pressure. The quantity is the same on paper, uptake per unit mass at a stated low partial pressure and temperature, and the values reported for comparable materials differ by margins too wide to read as scatter. The conflict tracks the measurement route. Gravimetric measurements, in which a sample takes up water from a stream of controlled humidity until its mass steadies, tend to report the higher values. Values inferred from breakthrough curves tend to come out lower, and the inference rests on the shape assumed for the mass-transfer zone, so part of the gap is built into the calculation rather than measured. Equilibration time is the second source of the conflict. At low partial pressure uptake is slow, and a measurement stopped at a fixed time records a point on the way to equilibrium in place of equilibrium itself. Papers differ in whether they waited for a steady reading, and the shorter tests read lower. Pretreatment is the third source: a sample regenerated harder before the test starts drier and takes up more, so the reported uptake partly records the regeneration the sample was given. Formed and crystal samples are also mixed in the comparisons, and the binder share alone moves the values. The disagreement is about method before it is about material. It cannot be settled from the published values, because the papers do not state their conditions on a common basis, and no two of the conflicting reports share route, equilibration rule, and pretreatment at once.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling: the water uptake of a formed adsorbent, measured again after the material has been regenerated many times under the conditions of its own duty. Papers report fresh uptake. Ageing studies report uptake after steaming, after storage, or after exposure to a contaminant. The cycled measurement, on the material that would actually be bought, under the regeneration the unit would actually apply, is missing. The gap matters because selection between the families turns on service life as much as on fresh capacity. A family with the higher fresh uptake and the faster cyclic loss can cost more over the life of a charge than a family that starts lower and holds its uptake, and at present that comparison cannot be made from measurements. Purchasers price the risk from warranty terms instead. A second gap follows from the first: no paper reports uptake and mechanical state together after cycling, so the balance between capacity loss and attrition loss in the same charge is unmeasured, and a bed can be retired for dust while its uptake is still sound, or held in service for its uptake while its dust loads the downstream equipment. Until the cycled measurement exists on a common basis, comparisons of the families rest on fresh material, and every judgement on selection in this review carries that limit.
